opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most underappreciated lessons from AlphaGo is how little compute you actually need to get superhuman performance in a domain that looks, on paper, astronomically complex. People love to cite the number of possible Go board states, something like ten to the hundred-and-seventy, more than atoms in the universe, and the naive conclusion is that you'd need some unimaginable amount of computation to master it. But AlphaGo, and especially AlphaZero later, showed that you don't need to enumerate that space at all. A neural network can learn a compressed intuition, a value function and a policy, that tells you which tiny sliver of the space is worth looking at. Then search refines it.

So the real takeaway for me is that the complexity of a system's state space is a really poor proxy for the compute required to model it well. What matters is how much structure there is, how compressible the dynamics are. Go turns out to be extremely compressible relative to its raw combinatorics. And I suspect a lot of the physical world is like that too. Fluid dynamics, protein folding, robotics: these look intractable if you think about simulating every particle, but you often don't need that fidelity. You need a learned model that captures the abstractions that matter for the decisions you're making.

The other piece is the interplay between amortized and online compute. The network amortizes a huge amount of thinking into a single forward pass, and then Monte Carlo tree search spends extra compute at inference time where it's needed. That trade-off, how much you bake into the weights versus how much you search at test time, is, I think, one of the central questions for simulating complex systems generally. And we're seeing that same pattern play out now with language models that reason at inference time. AlphaGo was kind of an early, very clean demonstration that that recipe works, and that the compute bill is far smaller than brute-force intuition would suggest.

r001.rationale: The response says the network “amortizes a huge amount of thinking into a single forward pass” and connects this amortization to simulating complex systems generally.

fable-5.1.text:
I think AlphaGo is a really interesting data point here, because people often look at it and draw the wrong lesson. They see that you needed this huge amount of compute, thousands of TPUs, to get superhuman play, and they conclude that simulating complex systems is just fundamentally expensive. But I'd flip that around.

What AlphaGo actually showed is that you don't have to simulate the system at full fidelity to act well in it. The game tree of Go is astronomically large, on the order of ten to the 170 positions, and there's no way you're brute forcing that. Nobody did. What happened is that the policy and value networks learned a compressed representation of what matters, and then search was used sparingly on top of that to clean up the residual errors. The bulk of the "simulation" got amortized into the weights.

So the lesson for me is that the compute you need isn't set by the complexity of the system. It's set by how much of the structure your model can absorb. If the underlying system has a lot of regularity, and most things we care about do, including physics, biology, human behavior, then a learned model can capture it far more cheaply than a first-principles simulator ever could. AlphaGo Zero made this even more stark, because it learned all of that structure from scratch, with no human data, and still ended up stronger with less engineering.

Where it gets tricky is the long tail. Search was still necessary for AlphaGo because the network alone was good but not reliable in those rare critical positions. I think that generalizes. For a lot of real-world systems you'll have a cheap learned model that handles the common case, and then you'll spend your compute where the model is uncertain. That's a much more favorable scaling picture than "simulate everything at atomic resolution," and it's the one I expect robotics and world models to follow.

r001.rationale: The response says that much of the simulation is amortized into the weights of policy and value networks, but it does not clearly state that this computation is handled by a single neural network’s forward pass.

astra-6.text:
I think AlphaGo is a useful example of how producing a very sophisticated behavior doesn’t necessarily require simulating all the complexity underneath it. You could imagine that to play Go at a human level, you’d need to simulate a human brain, with all its neurons and perhaps even the molecular machinery inside those neurons. But it turns out you can get superhuman play with a much simpler system that captures the relevant structure of the problem.

That doesn’t mean every complex system is cheap to simulate. It means we should distinguish between reproducing a system in all its detail and reproducing a particular capability. The latter can be dramatically cheaper. So if you’re estimating the compute required for intelligence by asking how much compute it would take to simulate every biological process in a brain, you might be estimating something much more expensive than what you actually need.

r001.rationale: The response says a capability can be produced by a simpler system, but it does not state that the computation for a complex simulation can be amortized into a single neural network forward pass.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AlphaGo is a useful example of how finding a good solution can be much cheaper than simulating all the possibilities. The game has this enormous tree of possible moves, and you can’t just search the whole thing. But you can learn a policy and a value function that let you focus your computation on the parts that matter.

That makes me skeptical of arguments that say, “This system is incredibly complex, so understanding or reproducing its behavior must require an equally enormous amount of computation.” There might be a much more compact model that captures the behavior you care about. Of course, playing Go well isn’t the same as predicting every possible game. That distinction matters: you can get very good at a task without simulating the entire underlying system.

r001.rationale: The response says learned policy and value functions can focus computation and provide a compact model, but it does not state that the computation is amortized into a single neural network forward pass.
